## Result of this run

The strongest result I obtained is a **candidate theorem removing the inverse-success-probability barrier for a broad, explicitly defined class of heralded Gaussian optical experiments**.

The algorithmic conclusion depends on OpenAI family 113’s perfect-matching approximation theorem. The new work is a reduction, together with conditional-energy bounds, that makes that theorem applicable even when the optical event being conditioned on is exponentially rare. I extended the argument beyond the repository’s pure, undisplaced setting to **mixed and displaced Gaussian states**, then derived a quantitative extension allowing small phase errors.

This is not an independently validated historical-calibre breakthrough. It is a candidate computational-boundary theorem with a written proof, explicit resource accounting, and **712 exact checks**. The remaining barriers to a substantially stronger result are identified below.

## 1. The changed premise

The useful starting capital was **Astra N38**. It already records a classical sampler for the complete photon-count distribution of a pure Gaussian state with a nonnegative matrix. Its mechanism is an established loop-soup construction. Crucially, the card also identifies a limitation: conditioning that sampler on a rare photon pattern incurs an inverse-acceptance cost. The unconditioned distribution being easy to sample does not make an exponentially rare conditional distribution easy. 

That exposed a specific target:

> **Does rare photon-number postselection create a computational obstruction even when the underlying Gaussian amplitudes have a positive representation?**

The changed premise is OpenAI family 113’s stated fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme for counting perfect matchings in arbitrary graphs. Its contract includes relative—not merely additive—accuracy, exact detection of zero counts, and polynomial worst-case bit time, including unsuccessful random tapes. Those details are essential here.
